name: Adam Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and a junior developer on building-keypad software at a tech company, after locksmith work and a two-year college diploma. I never use AI tools and still have a senior check my code against a test lock. Livia, my partner, works in a school kitchen; our sons are grown, and our typical developer pay has helped us rent with about three months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the building-access team that a small AI shortcut may tidy help tickets, but the door must still open for the right resident. I do not use AI tools; I check our keypad software against a real test lock with the senior developer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58 and a junior after a two-year college diploma. Livia works in a school kitchen, our grown sons live elsewhere, and typical developer pay plus her wage have given us three months of rent and bills in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep testing each keypad release on the workshop lock and ask the senior to check my code. We would save 75 monthly while both wages arrive and repair our old table rather than buy another one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be calm about our own work and rent in this picture. A lock that works in a demonstration but traps a resident is no success.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a real lock?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I was a locksmith before taking the diploma, and a screen can say unlocked while the latch is still stuck. I want to hear the bolt move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why did you change work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands tired of emergency calls at night, so I tried software work. I am still learning the code and do not pretend the diploma made me senior.

say: I want **keypads tested** on a real lock before release.
I rely on **senior code review** for software changes.
think: I have **three months saved** from two current wages.
I see **rent covered** while the school kitchen and developer jobs continue.
do: **Keep testing keypads** with workshop lock and senior review.
**Save 75 monthly** while both wages arrive; repair old table instead of replacing it.
S0.quote: A lock that works in a demonstration but traps a resident is no success.
fieldNote: His **locksmith history** gives physical context, but he remains a junior at writing software.
The **three-month cushion** and two wages support calm without assuming grown sons will pay.

steps.text: Keep testing keypad releases on workshop lock with senior code review
Save 75 monthly while both household wages arrive
Repair old table rather than buy a replacement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking checking, booking, writing and coding could remove many simple keypad tickets from a junior’s desk. The company should tell us which safety decisions a named person still owns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours may shrink because I am still learning the software and fix the straightforward bugs. Three months saved is useful, but Livia’s school-kitchen pay will not cover our rent and bills alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the manager this month for written junior-hour plans and approved paid time with the hardware tester to learn how electronic lock failures are diagnosed. If approved, I’d practise on two broken test locks weekly; if my developer hours fall, I’d search paid local locksmith vacancies only if the wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my hours, and I would not hide that from Livia. I can learn from a broken latch without trusting an unexplained AI answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not use an AI coding tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used one and do not want an unfamiliar answer on a door that people need in a fire. I would first master a fault I can test by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Livia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show her the written hours plan when it arrives and compare our actual pay slips. We would not spend the three-month reserve on guesses.

say: I want **written junior hours** before the company cuts shifts.
I want **named safety decisions** on electronic doors.
think: I could lose **simple keypad tickets** and paid hours.
I cannot use **Livia’s kitchen wage** alone to pay rent.
do: **Request written hours** and practise broken-lock diagnosis only with approved paid tester time.
**Search paid locksmith vacancies** if developer hours fall and local wages cover rent and bills.
S1.quote: I can learn from a broken latch without trusting an unexplained AI answer.
fieldNote: He prefers **physical fault diagnosis** to an AI assistant he has never used.
His **paid testing practice** depends on manager approval; a job search begins only after reduced developer hours.

steps.text: Request written junior hours; practise two broken test locks weekly only with approved paid tester time
Search paid local locksmith vacancies if developer hours fall and wages cover rent and bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write our keypad code and answer building managers more cheaply than the junior team. Robots fitting locks and doing school-kitchen work may come around 2031, after our screen tasks change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my junior developer wage could end quickly. Livia’s wage and three months of savings would carry us briefly, but the old locksmith trade may have changed since I worked it full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d postpone replacing our worn sofa and ask for written notice of any developer cuts now. If my job ends after 2028, I’d apply for paid local locksmith openings only if vacancies exist, I can meet their current requirements and wages cover rent and bills; I would not buy a van before an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed at the speed of losing my pay. A key in my pocket is not a paid shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your sons help with rent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not budget for that. They have their own homes and work, and I need to know what Livia and I can cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a locksmith requires a new certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the employer funds it and pays for training time. I would not take a course fee from the rent reserve on the chance of a vacancy.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach keypad code first.
I expect **lock-fitting robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **junior wage** could end quickly.
I cannot assume **old locksmith experience** meets current hiring rules.
do: **Postpone sofa replacement** and request written cut notice now.
**Apply for locksmith work** after 2028 loss only if qualified local vacancies cover rent and bills.
S2.quote: A key in my pocket is not a paid shift.
fieldNote: He checks **current locksmith requirements** before calling the old trade a viable job.
A **van or course fee** would consume rent savings without an actual paid offer.

steps.text: Postpone worn-sofa replacement when developer cuts threaten
Apply for paid local locksmith vacancies if displaced after 2028, qualified and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us time to find out which building-access faults people still have to repair. Robots fitting locks may follow around 2034, later than the code changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could bring my locksmith knowledge up to date while the developer wage lasts, but I will not spend the three-month rent reserve on a course. I would need a paid place and a real certificate requirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask a local security installer whether it has a paid trainee vacancy for modern access controllers. If it offers paid supervised training, funds the required certificate and the wage covers rent and bills, I’d enrol; we would save 65 monthly while both wages hold, and after 2031 developer job loss I’d apply only for paid local access-repair vacancies I qualify for and whose wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my code role but glad to have time to learn a modern lock. A good apprenticeship has a wage on the day you turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would supervise you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An experienced access technician would need to check my wiring and the test door. I know old keys; I do not yet know every new controller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay the certificate fee yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not from our rent buffer. I would enrol only if the installer funds it and pays the training hours.

say: I want **paid controller training** before AGI reaches keypad code in 2031.
I expect **lock robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I can update **locksmith skills** on modern electronic controllers while my developer pay lasts.
I need **employer-funded certification** and supervised paid hours before changing trades.
do: **Enrol in access training** only with paid vacancy, supervised hours, funded certificate and bill-covering wage.
**Save 65 monthly** only while both wages hold.
**Apply for access-repair work** after 2031 loss only if qualified local paid vacancies cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious but determined** about a modern trade route.
S3.quote: A good apprenticeship has a wage on the day you turn up.
fieldNote: His **apprenticeship choice** requires a real paid opening, supervision and funded certification.
The **rent reserve** is not treated as money for an uncertain course fee.

steps.text: Enrol in paid supervised access-controller training only if vacancy funds certificate and wage covers bills
Save 65 monthly while both household wages continue
Apply for qualified paid local access-repair vacancies if displaced after 2031 and wages cover bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade before full AGI in 2036 gives families time to repair what they own and workers time to check real vacancies. Robots fitting locks and working in school kitchens may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may need paid work at 68; I have not verified a retirement amount, so I will not pretend the date settles our rent. Our three-month savings could grow if both wages keep arriving, though my junior role may still end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep testing the keypad software while the job pays and put 85 monthly into savings if both wages continue. I’d check paid access-controller trainee openings annually and enrol only with supervised paid time, funded certification and a wage covering rent and bills; if the developer role ends after 2036, I’d apply to qualified paid local access-repair vacancies only if wages cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be uneasy about work later but able to pay rent in the next few years. I want the cost of a door repair and the cost of training written down, not guessed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid placement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Livia and I cannot suspend rent while someone decides whether I am useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town for a job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would search the local installers and software employers. Livia’s school job and our community are here, so I am not making a move plan.

say: I want **written trainee costs** before AGI reaches keypad code in 2036.
I expect **lock robots around 2039** to follow later.
think: I cannot assume **retirement income** without a verified figure.
I might grow **three months saved** if both wages last.
do: **Keep testing keypads** while the developer role pays.
**Save 85 monthly** while both wages hold; enrol only if paid supervised trainee vacancy funds certificate and covers bills.
**Apply for access repair** after 2036 loss only if qualified local vacancies cover bills.
feel: **Uneasy later**, secure in rent payments now.
S4.quote: I want the cost of a door repair and the cost of training written down, not guessed.
fieldNote: He refuses **unpaid placements** and unverified retirement amounts despite a decade of warning.
The **modern access route** stays conditional on actual local paid training and qualified vacancies.

steps.text: Keep testing keypad software while junior developer role remains paid
Save 85 monthly while both household wages continue

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my junior developer pay could end before a current paid locksmith opening appears. Written notice and a real local job that covers rent would help us protect our savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether I would ask my sons to fund our rent. I would not write my grown sons’ wages into a rent plan for my partner Livia and me.

headlineQuote: I would not write my grown sons’ wages into a rent plan for my partner Livia and me.
portrait: Adam is a **58-year-old junior developer** with a two-year diploma, typical pay and three months saved.
He and Livia **rent** while their grown sons run their own homes.
He **never uses AI** and tests building-access code against a physical lock.
He considers **paid access training** only with supervision, funded certification and bill-covering wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his junior wage before a qualified paid locksmith vacancy appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written cut notice** and a real local rent-covering locksmith opening would help.
